malnutrition in mCRC patients is associated with greater drug-induced toxicity and shorter overall survival.
malnourished mCRC patients have a poorer response to chemotherapy, more severe toxicities, and shorter survival.
malnutrition is common in mCRC and is associated with increased chemotherapy-related toxicity and reduced survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nutritional status of patients with colorectal cancer.
the nutritional status in metastatic colorectal patients and the possible influence on the efficacy of chemotherapy.
the nutritional status of metastatic colorectal carcinoma patients and the relationship between nutritional status and the tolerability and survival of these patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NRI is a useful and reliable tool in the assessment of nutritional status of patients with mCRC, and the results of this study suggest a possible role for NRI in the management of these patients.
malnutrition is an important prognostic factor in mCRC patients and that nutritional intervention should be considered as a standard of care in this patient population.
malnutrition is associated not only with worse prognosis but also with greater toxicity of chemotherapy in mCRC patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nutritional status is a prognostic factor in mCRC patients.
the nutritional status of mCRC patients should be assessed at the time of cancer diagnosis, and that nutritional support should be provided to patients with severe malnutrition.
malnutrition is common in mCRC patients, is associated with worse outcomes and should be routinely evaluated and addressed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
malnutrition is common in mCRC patients, is a risk factor for poor tolerance to chemotherapy and may affect overall survival.
the nutritional status of patients with metastatic colorectal carcinoma should be assessed before treatment initiation and nutritional support should be offered when necessary.
